summary: This standards-track document extends how OSPFv3 Link State Advertisements are formatted, going beyond the fixed format of RFC 5340. Without it, attributes of links and IPv6 prefixes have to be advertised in separate LSAs and matched up. The extension makes OSPFv3 easier to extend.

plainLanguage.summary: A form with fixed boxes has no room for new facts. This gives OSPFv3 a roomier form so new details can be added neatly.

questions: what is the ospfv3 extended lsa format
how to migrate ospfv3 to extended lsas
subtitle: A TLV-based LSA format that lets OSPFv3 carry new link and prefix information without separate side LSAs.

tldr.problem: OSPFv3 LSAs have a fixed format, so extra attributes of links and IPv6 prefixes had to go into separate LSAs that routers then had to correlate with the fixed-format ones.
tldr.mechanism: Each fixed-format LSA gets an Extended counterpart (function code plus 32) whose body is a list of Type-Length-Value tuples, so existing information and new information travel in the same LSA.
tldr.outcome: OSPFv3 can be extended by adding TLVs and sub-TLVs, with rules for ignoring unknown ones and for migrating from Legacy LSAs, and two new IANA registries for TLV and sub-TLV types.

facts.label: TLV alignment
facts.value: 4 octets; padding not counted in Length

today: RFC 8362 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It updates RFC 5340 and RFC 5838.

sections.title: Why Extend OSPFv3 LSAs
sections.content:
OSPFv3 needs functional extension beyond what the fixed-format Link State Advertisement (LSA) of RFC 5340 can readily support. Without it, attributes of OSPFv3 links and advertised IPv6 prefixes must be advertised in separate LSAs and correlated to the fixed-format ones.

This document encodes the existing LSA information in Type-Length-Value (TLV) tuples and allows more information in additional TLVs. It updates RFC 5340 and RFC 5838 by giving TLV-based encodings for base OSPFv3 and for address family support. Extra requirements named include source/destination routing and route tagging, and an earlier multi-topology routing proposal was a similar extension.

A final requirement is to limit changes to those needed for TLV-based LSAs. Semantics and details such as the IPv6 prefix representation are mostly retained, to speed adoption. The RFC calls the new TLV-based LSAs Extended LSAs and the fixed-format ones Legacy LSAs.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers tell each other about the roads they know. The old message form had no room for extra notes, so notes went on separate papers. This RFC adds a form with space for notes.

sections.title: Extended LSA Types
sections.content:
Backward compatibility needs new LSA codes. RFC 5340 defines eight fixed-format LSAs. Each Extended LSA uses the same function code as its Legacy twin plus 32 (0x20), which eases implementation and debugging. The alternative, a bit in the LS Type marking the new format, would have used half of the function code space.

The U-bit MUST be set in the LS Type, so routers that do not understand an Extended LSA still flood it. The table lists the types. Function code 38 is unused and not to be allocated.
sections.plainLanguage: Each old message type gets a new twin with a number 32 higher, and the twin is marked as pass-it-on so older routers hand it along even if they cannot read it.

sections.title: The TLV Format
sections.content:
TLVs inside Extended LSAs use the same format as the Traffic Engineering extensions to OSPF (RFC 3630). The variable section is one or more nested TLV tuples; nested ones are sub-TLVs. Each starts with a 16-bit Type and a 16-bit Length, then the value.

Length counts only the value, in octets. The TLV is padded to 4-octet alignment and the padding is not counted: a 3-octet value has Length 3 but takes 8 octets in total. Nested TLVs are also 32-bit aligned. TLVs and sub-TLVs MAY occur in any order, and each specification defines whether one is required and what happens with repeats.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note has a label, a size, and then the note itself. Notes are packed in neat 4-byte boxes, with blank space added if a note does not fill its box.

sections.title: The TLVs and the Extended LSAs
sections.content:
Eight top-level TLVs and three sub-TLVs are defined. Each is valid only in certain LSAs; if it shows up elsewhere it MUST be ignored. The Router-Link TLV describes one router link and lives in the E-Router-LSA. The Attached-Routers TLV lists the routers on a multi-access network and lives in the E-Network-LSA. The Inter-Area-Prefix and Inter-Area-Router TLVs go in the matching inter-area LSAs, and the External-Prefix TLV goes in the E-AS-External-LSA and E-NSSA-LSA. The Intra-Area-Prefix TLV and the IPv6 and IPv4 Link-Local Address TLVs go in the E-Link-LSA, and the first also in the E-Intra-Area-Prefix-LSA.

For external routes, the forwarding address and the external route tag become sub-TLVs of the External-Prefix TLV. The Referenced LS Type and Referenced Link State ID were never used, so they are omitted. Only the first instance of each such sub-TLV is used; later ones MUST be ignored.

The Inter-Area-Prefix, Inter-Area-Router and E-AS-External LSAs each MUST contain a single matching TLV, which keeps semantics and incremental SPF computation as before. The E-Link-LSA and E-Intra-Area-Prefix-LSA may carry multiple Intra-Area-Prefix TLVs, and the Referenced LS Type of the latter MUST be an E-Router-LSA (0xA021) or an E-Network-LSA (0xA022).

The RFC also extends the prefix options. The LA-bit SHOULD be set in Inter-Area-Prefix TLVs and MAY be set in External-Prefix TLVs for a host address that is an interface address. A new N-bit (value 0x20) marks a host address that identifies the advertising router, as a hint to the preferred address for reaching it. The RFC names Node Segment Identifiers in Segment Routing as one use.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of message has a matching slot type, like a form where the name goes in the name box. New or odd slots are simply skipped by routers that do not know them.

sections.title: Malformed LSAs and Unknown TLVs
sections.content:
An Extended LSA with an inconsistent length or other encoding errors MUST NOT be installed in the Link State Database, acknowledged or flooded. Such LSAs SHOULD be counted or logged for the administrator. An LSA is also malformed if a required TLV or sub-TLV is missing. A TLV is not invalid merely because it has extra content: it is invalid only if its length exceeds the LSA or is below the minimum for that TLV.

Section 6.3 sets general rules so future TLVs stay compatible. Unrecognized TLVs and sub-TLVs are ignored. A new TLV's document MUST say whether partial deployment is supported, and either how to prevent deployment or how to handle it. A recognized TLV that is too short makes the LSA malformed, and it SHOULD NOT be acknowledged. Future TLVs must be optional.
sections.plainLanguage: If a form is broken or missing a needed box, throw it away and write down that it happened. If it just has extra boxes you do not understand, ignore those and read the rest.

sections.title: Migrating from Legacy LSAs
sections.content:
Backward compatibility here means only the ability of a router to receive, process and originate the Extended LSAs. There are two modes. In full migration, enabling the global parameter ExtendedLSASupport makes the router originate Extended LSAs and use them for SPF computation. Areas can be migrated one by one with AreaExtendedLSASupport, while Legacy AS-External-LSAs are still originated and used. A domain or area can also migrate without disruption by running separate OSPFv3 instances for Extended LSAs, first with higher administrative distance, then preferred once the RIBs are verified, and finally dropping the Legacy instance.

In sparse mode, OSPFv3 keeps using Legacy LSAs for SPF and originates Extended LSAs only for new functionality, with just the top-level TLVs that functionality needs. This lets new functions be added to an existing domain without migration. For regular areas, disabling AreaExtendedLSASupport while ExtendedLSASupport is enabled is contradictory and SHOULD be prohibited by implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: You can switch a whole town to the new forms bit by bit, or just use the new forms only for the new jobs while everything else stays on the old forms.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
Nine Extended LSA types were added to the OSPFv3 LSA Function Codes registry, and the value 0x20 was assigned to the N-bit in the OSPFv3 Prefix-Options registry. Two new registries cover TLVs and sub-TLVs. Their code points are common to all Extended LSAs.

The TLV registry has nine values allocated (0 through 8, with 0 Reserved). The sub-TLV registry has four (0 through 3, with 0 Reserved). In both, 9-32767 (TLVs) and 4-32767 (sub-TLVs) are allocated by IETF Review or IESG Approval, 32768-33023 are reserved for experimental use, 33024-45055 are first come first served, and 45056-65535 are not to be assigned at this time.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of label numbers. Low numbers need careful approval, some are for experiments, some go to whoever asks first, and the top ones are kept empty for now.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Extensible OSPFv3 LSAs face the same security concerns as RFC 5340. In addition, implementations must make sure that malformed TLV and sub-TLV permutations do not cause hard OSPFv3 failures.

The RFC adds that if digital signing of OSPFv3 LSAs were ever required, as RFC 2154 describes for OSPFv2, the mechanisms here would greatly simplify the extension.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers must not crash when handed a messy form. Same safety rules as before apply.
